title: The First Emperor Burns the Books
text:
In 221 BC the king of Qin conquered the last of his rivals and became Qin Shi Huang, the First Emperor of a unified China. His chancellor, Li Si, helped him replace the old feudal states with a centralized system of provinces.

In 213 BC, according to the historian Sima Qian, a scholar named Chunyu Yue spoke at a court banquet and urged the emperor to follow the ancient model of granting fiefs to his sons, warning that anything not modeled on antiquity would not last. Li Si answered that scholars who used the past to criticize the present were confusing the people. He proposed that the histories of the other states be burned, that private copies of the classic Book of Songs and Book of Documents be handed over and burned, and that anyone who discussed them or used the past to criticize the present be executed. Books on medicine, divination and agriculture were spared. The emperor approved.

The next year, Sima Qian says, the emperor had more than four hundred and sixty scholars put to death for criticizing him.

The dynasty did not last. The First Emperor died in 210 BC, Li Si was executed in a court intrigue, and the Qin collapsed in 206 BC.
lesson: Silencing critics removes the warnings you most need. A leader who cannot bear to hear the past questioned cannot see the future coming.
people: Qin Shi Huang, Li Si, Chunyu Yue
source: Sima Qian, Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian), chapters 6 and 87
caveat: Some historians think Han writers exaggerated the scale of the burning and the killing of scholars to discredit the Qin.
